_comment: Canned replies for --dry-run. A list is played in order, one item per earlier turn by the same speaker.

key_hypotheses: The job hypothesis describes a real, recent struggle, not a general wish
The current workaround costs time, accuracy or independence
The current workaround is good enough and nothing would change
prep.interviewee_profile: Someone in this segment who has done a leveling task in the last month. Screen out anyone who has never done one.
starter_questions: Tell me about the last time you had to get something level.
What made that the day you did it?
Who else was around while you worked?
How did you know it was straight?
When did you find out whether it really was level?
contrasting_questions: Was the bigger problem the time it took or the result?
Why that method rather than asking someone for help?
What's worse about your current method than the one before it?
Would you rather it be faster or more accurate?

interviewer.question: Tell me about the last time you had to get something level.
How did you know it was straight?
What did you do when it turned out to be off?

user: It was a set of shelves a couple of weeks ago. I'd put it off for a while, then finally did it on a Saturday morning.
I used the level app on my phone and checked it twice. Honestly I wasn't completely sure until someone else looked at it.
I took the bracket down, moved it a bit and redid one screw. It added maybe half an hour, which was annoying but not the end of the world.

debrief.about_me_and_goals: Handles small jobs around the house and puts them off until a free morning. Wants to finish a job once without redoing it.

most_pressing_needs.need: Know the job is level without waiting for someone else to check
Avoid redoing work after it turns out to be off

main_insights.insight: The phone app is trusted only up to a point; a second opinion still decides when the job is done
A redo costs about half an hour, which is annoying but tolerable

current_solutions: Asking someone to look at it
opportunities: Confidence at the moment of fixing, not after
The current approach may be good enough for small jobs

advocate.summary: The debrief matches the transcript, and the interviewee named a cost and a workaround. The pain is mild: a redo costs half an hour, so the job may not be strong enough to change behavior.
verify_in_real_interviews: How often does a redo actually happen?
Would they stop asking for a second check if a tool told them it was level?

shared_jobs.job: Finish a small fixing job once, without waiting for someone else to confirm it
shared_jobs.evidence: Both debriefs name a second check by another person as the moment the job is really done.

strongest_segment.why: Depending on someone else to confirm the work is a repeated cost the interviewee wants gone.

weakest_segment.why: A redo costs little, and the current approach is described as good enough.

claims_to_verify: How often a second check is actually needed
Whether a sound would be trusted over a person's eyes
